title: Swiss spring-date intervals covered 81% of 2015-2024 outcomes but missed mainly early dates
abstract: We tested whether climate-response prediction intervals kept their coverage in later years. We used published annual anomalies for 19 Swiss spring plant phases, eight later phases, 43 British butterfly timing series and 36 butterfly growth series. Models were fitted through 2004. Residual ranges from 2005-2014 gave frozen intervals for 2015-2024. Total coverage was 79-85%, near the 81.8% exchangeable-rank reference. Yet spring intervals missed 34 early outcomes and only two late outcomes in 190 phase-years. Rolling ten-year updates reduced these to 22 and ten, made intervals narrower, and lowered spring interval score by 15.1%. About 78% of that score gain came from center changes. Rolling climate intervals had 43.4% lower spring score than a rolling outcome-range baseline. Updates raised later-plant scores and gave no clear butterfly score gain. Older fitted models supported the spring update result in the same late test years, but not in an earlier decade. The exploratory tail test had permutation p=0.017 before and 0.067 after correction over four groups. Thus total coverage can hide directional misses, but this short test does not prove a general calibration defect. Limits include ten test years, shared weather, changing site coverage, annual averages and observed target-year weather. This is a retrospective uncertainty audit, not a new interval method or an advance weather forecast test. Code, input hashes, group results and reproduction instructions are included.
